À Montréal, les municipales 2025 ont mis: In Montréal’s 2025 municipal elections, the absence of young people and marginalized neighbourhoods at the ballot box was plain to see.
Candidat·e·s lors des élections municipa: Candidates in the 2025 Montréal municipal elections. Photo credit: La Converse montage
Le lendemain du scrutin municipal, j’ai: The day after the municipal vote, I wanted to know who had voted – and, above all, who hadn’t made it to the polls. From Parc-Extension to Saint-Michel, from Saint-Léonard to Montréal-Nord, I met candidates, community workers and young citizens. Each of them, in their own way, describes the same absence: that of a political voice in working-class neighbourhoods.
Leur constat n’accuse personne. Il montr: Their assessment doesn’t blame anyone. It simply shows how uneven civic education, local representation and trust in institutions remain in Montréal. And how, behind every missing vote, there is often a story of distance, of mistrust… or of hope that is still fragile.
<strong>Lendemain de vote à Montréal. Le: The day after the vote in Montréal. Posters are still hanging on street corners, Soraya Martinez Ferrada’s face presides over the utility poles, and Ensemble Montréal and its leader now run the metropolis.
À la Maison du citoyen de Saint-Michel,: At the Maison du citoyen de Saint-Michel, a young community worker adjusts the microphones in a small music studio. Between recordings, Riyadh Amokrane talks about voting, trust and disillusionment. Two days after the November 2 municipal elections, his office is quiet. Montréal has just changed its political course, but 63% of voters, Riyadh among them, stayed away from the polls.
Aux élections municipales du 2 novembre,: In the November 2 municipal elections, only 37.02% of Montrealers exercised their right to vote. It was a historically low rate, which fell below 25% in several working-class neighbourhoods.
À LaSalle, le district Cecil-P.-Newman a: In LaSalle, the Cecil-P.-Newman district recorded a turnout of 23.47%. In Saint-Michel, barely 24.07% of voters cast a ballot. In Pierrefonds-Roxboro, an outlying borough that, like many Montréal neighbourhoods, <l1>has a high percentage of families living in poverty</l1>, turnout peaked at 28%. <l2>According to figures</l2> from Élections Québec, the poorest, youngest and most culturally diverse neighbourhoods are the ones that vote the least.
Derrière la victoire de Soraya Martinez: Behind Soraya Martinez Ferrada’s victory, one question remains: who elected the new mayor? And who chose not to? Residents and former candidates speak out.
<strong>« Je voulais voter, mais je n’ai: “I wanted to vote, but I didn’t push it”
Riyadh Amokrane, qui est âgé de 30 ans,: Riyadh Amokrane, 30, works in violence prevention at the Maison du citoyen de Saint-Michel. In the studio he runs, <l1>La Zone LCSM</l1>, young people come to record their music, or simply to talk.
Le 2 novembre, il comptait voter pour la: On November 2, he planned to vote for the first time, in Montréal-Nord, where he lives. “I knew a candidate in Saint-Michel,” he says. “He had asked me to vote for a friend in Montréal-Nord. But on voting day, I couldn’t find my voter card.”
Riyadh aurait pu chercher, appeler, insi: Riyadh could have looked for it, called, pushed. He didn’t. “I didn’t feel pushed to go any further. It’s as if something inside me was pulling me back toward inaction,” he confides.
Riyadh Amokrane, intervenant à la Maison: Riyadh Amokrane, community worker at the Maison du citoyen de Saint-Michel. Photo credit: Nouri Nesrouche
Ce « quelque chose », il l’explique par: He explains this “something” by the distance that separates him from institutions: “Ever since we were little, anything institutional scares us. It’s not a fear of the system, no. It’s really a fear of belonging to a system that doesn’t look like us […] We have nothing to do with politics. It’s a world of hypocrites, so to speak.”
Cette déconnexion, il l’observe chaque j: He sees this disconnect every day: “The young people here feel far removed from all that. They don’t see municipal politics as something that affects them. Even I understood late what the City does. This lack of information is serious!”
Selon Riyadh, les campagnes de mobilisat: According to Riyadh, mobilization campaigns often miss their target. “We put up posters, run contests, launch campaigns, but that’s not what works. What we need is human contact,” he says. He then gives an example: “The only one I saw come and talk to us naturally in the neighbourhood was Éric Allen, an approachable candidate [from the Action Montréal party, editor’s note]. That’s what we need.”
Malgré la désillusion, Riyadh conserve u: Despite the disillusionment, Riyadh holds on to one conviction: “I tell young people that voting matters. But we have to start believing again that this system belongs to us a little.”
<strong>« Ils pensent que le vote munici: “They think the municipal vote isn’t that important”
À Saint-Léonard, le taux de participatio: In Saint-Léonard, turnout did not exceed 30%. “It’s mostly seniors, often of Italian origin, who vote,” observes Azzouz Abdellah, 27, a former Projet Montréal candidate. Still mulling over the 11.9% of the vote he received, despite being well rooted among young people and the Maghrebi community, he looks back on the obstacles he ran into during the campaign: “Young people, especially in the Maghrebi community, think the municipal vote isn’t that important.”
Pendant six semaines, Azzouz affirme avo: For six weeks, Azzouz says, he knocked on hundreds of doors. “Many told me they were going to vote. On election day, they didn’t show up. They say yes to be polite, but they don’t really believe in change,” he believes.
Selon lui, la<l1> faiblesse du taux de p: In his view, <l1>the low turnout of the Maghrebi community in Saint-Léonard</l1> [the largest group, with about 20,000 residents] also stems from a lack of cohesion: “We’re not yet a 100% tight-knit community. Some people vote based on the candidate’s origin, not on their platform.”
Malgré la défaite, Azzouz reste détermin: Despite the defeat, Azzouz remains determined and is already thinking about the next step, perhaps even the next election, he says. “I want to keep making things move. Maybe in a different way.”
À Montréal-Nord, seulement 27,99 % des é: In Montréal-Nord, only 27.99% of voters cast a ballot. Action Montréal’s candidate for borough mayor, Anastasia Marcelin, saw the reasons for this abstention up close. “People complain, but they don’t get up,” she says bluntly.
Son engagement, elle le décrit comme un: She describes her involvement as an act of resistance. “I’m an activist, I’m a fighter. It was a tragic event – a young person assaulted by a police officer – that pushed me to run,” says M<sup>s</sup>. Marcelin. A community activist and entrepreneur, she campaigned in the streets among residents who were often wary. “I met young people who were working at the polling stations: not one of them had voted,” she says, astonished.
M<sup>me</sup> Marcelin explique ce phén: M<sup>s</sup>. Marcelin attributes the phenomenon to a lack of electoral education. “People get lost. They mix up the municipal parties with the Liberals. We have to start again from the ground up, in schools, universities, communities.” For her, the solution lies in teaching and in the long term: “If we don’t do electoral education, Montréal-Nord will stay locked. We have four years to change that.” “Many residents come from countries where voting isn’t a habit,” she notes.
À Saint-Michel, les efforts de mobilisat: In Saint-Michel, mobilization efforts weren’t enough to <l1>break the electoral silence and quench the thirst to be listened to</l1>. Vivre Saint-Michel en santé (VSMS) and other community organizations stepped up their election cafés, meetings and debates. But the mobilization didn’t extend beyond the walls of the community organizations.
Naïma Mehennek, candidate de Transition: Naïma Mehennek, Transition Montréal’s candidate for city councillor in the François-Perrault district, experienced this first-hand. Having worked in the community sector for 20 years, she knows the realities of her neighbourhood. Her candidacy, she says, “was a way of extending that commitment.”
« Je me suis dit : “Si je peux m’asseoir: “I told myself: ‘If I can sit at a table where there is power and decisions are made, I could make our voices heard,’” says M<sup>s</sup>. Mehennek. Her efforts didn’t bear fruit. “People don’t know about municipal elections. They don’t know what a city councillor is for. And many aren’t citizens, or don’t believe their vote can change anything,” she says.
M<sup>me</sup> Mehennek parle d’un désin: M<sup>s</sup>. Mehennek speaks of a disinterest that, for many, is tied to their migration struggles. “It’s a disengagement they bring with them. They don’t believe in politics,” she stresses.
Mais elle y voit aussi une responsabilit: But she also sees a collective responsibility: “If we don’t take an interest in politics, politics takes an interest in us. The decisions we have to live with are the result of that absence.”
<strong>« Les gens ne savent pas à quoi: “People don’t know what the City is for”
À Parc-Extension, le constat est le même: In Parc-Extension, the observation is the same. <l1>Abdul-Razik Khan</l1>, 29, grew up there before opening a restaurant and a charity. A Transition Montréal candidate for city councillor, he collected only 736 votes. Met at Mama Khan, the Pakistani restaurant he runs on Saint-Denis Street, Abdul-Razik keeps smiling and stays clear-eyed. “A lot of people can’t vote. They’re newcomers, without citizenship,” he explains. But even those who can don’t always do it: “When I talk to them about city council, a lot of them tell me they don’t know what it’s for,” he adds.
Ses réflexions font écho à celles de ses: His thoughts echo those of his fellow former candidates. “It’s a political education problem. People vote in provincial or federal elections, but not in municipal ones, because they don’t see the direct connection.”
Il aurait pu cibler davantage les aînés: He could have targeted seniors more during his campaign, as some advised him to, but he preferred to talk to young people. “I want them to see themselves in someone like them. I work, I live in the neighbourhood. That’s what they want to see,” he says.
<strong>Entre désillusion et promesse d’: Between disillusionment and the promise of the future
De Saint-Michel à Parc-Extension, de Mon: From Saint-Michel to Parc-Extension, from Montréal-Nord to Saint-Léonard, a few findings emerge from the testimonies: seniors vote, young people abstain; immigrant communities distrust a system they know little about; poor neighbourhoods take little part in democratic life.
Chez celles et ceux qu’on a rencontrés,: Among those we met, despite the weariness, something like the beginning of hope shines through. Those who lost say they want to stay involved. Those who didn’t vote are already talking about starting to get informed. It’s not yet a movement, but it’s a sign.
Le salut viendra peut-être d’un candidat: Salvation may come from a Zohran Mamdani-style candidate – that young socialist elected mayor of New York, that son of immigrants who knew how to speak the language of everyday life – or perhaps it will come from even closer: from a young person turning on a mic in Saint-Michel, from a mother explaining the vote to her child, from a defeated candidate who keeps knocking on doors.
Partout à Montréal, des initiatives loca: All over Montréal, local initiatives are trying to bring residents closer to democratic life, far from election slogans.
· L’organisme<l1> L’apathie c’est plate<: · The organization <l1>L’apathie c’est plate</l1> works toward “a Canada where every young person is an agent of change in their daily life, and is meaningfully involved and included at every level of democracy.”
· <strong>À Saint-Michel</strong>, l’org: · In Saint-Michel, the organization Vivre Saint-Michel en santé is stepping up civic education workshops in schools as well as election cafés.
· <strong>À Montréal-Nord</strong>, l’or: · In Montréal-Nord, the organization Parole d’excluEs takes a citizen mobilization approach, centred on empowerment.
· <strong>Dans plusieurs arrondissements: · In several boroughs, organizations such as Concertation Montréal and CentrElles support newcomers in their civic steps, notably by translating election platforms and explaining the role of city council.
· Enfin, des initiatives indépendantes,: · Finally, independent initiatives, such as the podcast <l1>Les voix du quartier</l1> or the Maison du citoyen’s open mics, offer another space for political expression, more accessible and less institutional.
Ces expériences ne feront pas grimper le: These experiments won’t push up the turnout rate overnight. But they are a reminder that municipal democracy is often rebuilt at street level.
